notes.front: What is Long Term Evolution (LTE)?
notes.back: A mobile broadband communication standard defined by the 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP); a fourth-generation (4G) cellular technology.
notes.explanation: 3GPP is a worldwide standards development organisation.
notes.example: Like the 4G signal a phone uses for mobile data when there is no Wi-Fi around.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-187, Guide to LTE Security, 2 Overview of LTE Technology, p. 10
notes.evidence: LTE is a mobile broadband communication standard defined by the 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP), a worldwide standards development organization.

notes.front: What is near-field communication (NFC)?
notes.back: A form of short-range wireless communication based on the radio frequency identification set of standards.
notes.explanation: Mobile payment technology commonly relies on NFC, which has driven a large increase in its use.
notes.example: Like tapping a phone on a shop’s card reader to pay, rather than pairing it over Bluetooth.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-124 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise, Mobile Communication Mechanisms and Other Common Mobile Components, p. 18
notes.evidence: Another form of short-range wireless communication is NFC, which is typically optimized for distances of less than 4 inches but may be vulnerable at greater distances. NFC is based on the radio frequency identification (RFID) set of standards. Mobile payment technology commonly relies on NFC

notes.front: What is the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP)?
notes.back: A framework for adding arbitrary authentication methods to any protocol in a standardised way.
notes.explanation: Being a framework, it is not itself a single authentication method.
notes.example: Like a universal plug adaptor: the socket stays the same while different plugs (authentication methods) fit into it.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 3.3.2 Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP), p. 44
notes.evidence: EAP is a framework for adding arbitrary authentication methods in a standardized way to any protocol.

notes.front: In pre-shared key (PSK) authentication, what does each end of the communication hold?
notes.back: The identity of the other end and the shared secret key.
notes.explanation: NIST notes it is often deployed because it is the easiest method to configure: no public keys, certificates or EAP infrastructure are needed.
notes.example: Like a club where members get in by saying a password everyone was told in advance.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 3.3.4 Pre-shared Secret Key (PSK) Authentication, p. 45
notes.evidence: PSK-based authentication is often deployed because it is the easiest to configure. Each end of the communication has the identity of the other end and their PSK. It does not require generating public keys or certificates or running an EAP infrastructure.

notes.front: What is Wi-Fi Protected Access (WPA)?
notes.back: The Wi-Fi Alliance’s interim security solution, published in October 2002, while the 802.11i standard was finalised; stronger than Wired Equivalent Privacy.
notes.explanation: It was essentially a subset of the draft 802.11i requirements available at the time.
notes.example: Like a temporary bridge put up while the permanent one is still being built.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), 5.1.1 WLAN Standards, p. 51
notes.evidence: While IEEE was working on finalizing the 802.11i standard, the Alliance created an interim solution called Wi-Fi Protected Access (WPA). Published in October 2002, WPA is essentially a subset of the draft IEEE 802.11i requirements available at that time. WPA provides stronger security for WLAN communications than WEP.

notes.front: What is Wi-Fi Protected Access 2 (WPA2)?
notes.back: The Wi-Fi Alliance’s term for interoperable equipment capable of supporting the 802.11i requirements.
notes.explanation: It followed the ratification of 802.11i and offers stronger security controls than either WPA or Wired Equivalent Privacy.
notes.example: Like the permanent bridge opening once the full design was approved, replacing the temporary one.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), 5.1.1 WLAN Standards, p. 52
notes.evidence: with the ratification of the IEEE 802.11i amendment, the Wi-Fi Alliance introduced WPA2, its term for interoperable equipment that is capable of supporting IEEE 802.11i requirements. WPA2 offers stronger security controls than either WPA or WEP.

notes.front: What changes in Wi-Fi Protected Access 3 (WPA3) compared with the pre-shared key of earlier versions?
notes.back: The pre-shared key is replaced by a password-authenticated key exchange; WPA3 also offers perfect forward secrecy.
notes.explanation: NIST says the password-authenticated exchange offers more protection against the use of weak passwords.
notes.example: Like replacing a door code that anyone overhearing could reuse with a handshake that proves you know the code without saying it aloud.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, Link-layer protection for Wi-Fi, p. 104
notes.evidence: In WPA3, the PSK is replaced by Password Authenticated Key Exchange (PAKE), which offers more protection against the use of weak passwords. WPA3 also offers PFS.

notes.front: What is a rogue base station in cellular networks?
notes.back: An unlicensed base station, not owned by a genuine mobile network operator, broadcasting a network that masquerades as a legitimate carrier.
notes.explanation: The hardware can be bought cheaply off the shelf, and 2G base station software is freely available.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-187, Guide to LTE Security, 4.2 Rogue Base Stations, p. 32
notes.evidence: Rogue base stations are unlicensed base stations that are not owned and operated by an authentic MNO. They broadcast a cellular network masquerading as a legitimate carrier network. The necessary hardware to construct these devices can be inexpensively obtained using commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) hardware.

notes.front: Rogue base stations exploit the fact that handsets attach to whichever base station broadcasts as their preferred carrier and transmits at the {{c1::highest power level}}.
notes.explanation: So a rogue station need only pose as the preferred carrier and transmit strongly.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-187, Guide to LTE Security, 4.2 Rogue Base Stations, p. 32
notes.evidence: Rogue base stations exploit the fact that mobile handsets will attach to whichever base station is broadcasting as its preferred carrier network and is transmitting at the highest power level.

notes.front: In an LTE downgrade attack, what does the attacker force the user onto, and why is that dangerous?
notes.back: An older 2G or 3G network; the 2G air-interface cryptographic algorithms have significant weaknesses.
notes.explanation: The 3G algorithms had no significant publicly known weaknesses when NIST wrote.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-187, Guide to LTE Security, 4.2.2 Downgrade Attacks, p. 33
notes.evidence: an attacker can force a user to downgrade to either GSM or UMTS. As of the time of this writing, there are no significant, publicly known weaknesses in the cryptographic algorithms used to protect the confidentiality and integrity of the UMTS air interface. Unfortunately, significant weaknesses exist for the 2G GSM cryptographic algorithms

notes.front: A security team wants staff phones to resist rogue base station downgrade attacks. What does NIST say would help, if users could choose it?
notes.back: B: an option to connect only to 4G LTE networks, gaining mutual authentication.
notes.choices:
A) Turning up the phone’s transmit power
B) An option to connect only to 4G LTE networks, gaining mutual authentication
C) Using NFC instead of cellular data
D) Preferring 2G networks for their simplicity
notes.choicesExplained: A does not stop the phone attaching to a stronger rogue signal. C is a short-range technology, not a substitute for cellular. D is what the attacker wants: 2G lacks mutual authentication.
notes.explanation: Rogue base stations often exploit the lack of mutual authentication in 2G networks, which LTE’s authentication provides.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-187, Guide to LTE Security, 5.4 User-Defined Option for Connecting to LTE Networks, p. 38
notes.evidence: Rogue base stations often exploit the lack of mutual authentication that exists in GSM. Current mobile devices do not provide average users the option to ensure that a user's mobile device only connects to a 4G LTE network

notes.front: NFC is typically optimised for distances of less than {{c1::4 inches}}, but may be vulnerable at greater distances.
notes.explanation: The short design range is not a guarantee: NIST warns that attacks may work from further away.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-124 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise, Mobile Communication Mechanisms and Other Common Mobile Components, p. 18
notes.evidence: NFC, which is typically optimized for distances of less than 4 inches but may be vulnerable at greater distances.

notes.front: A café lets customers pay by holding a phone a few centimetres from the till reader. Which wireless technology does NIST say mobile payment commonly relies on?
notes.back: A: near-field communication.
notes.choices:
A) Near-field communication
B) Wi-Fi
C) LTE
D) Satellite positioning
notes.choicesExplained: C is cellular broadband. B is a wireless local area network technology. D gives location and does not carry payments.
notes.explanation: NFC is short-range and based on radio frequency identification standards, and mobile payment commonly relies on it.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-124 Rev. 2, Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise, Mobile Communication Mechanisms and Other Common Mobile Components, p. 18
notes.evidence: NFC is based on the radio frequency identification (RFID) set of standards. Mobile payment technology commonly relies on NFC

notes.front: Which Wi-Fi security protocol was deprecated in 2004 in favour of WPA, and why?
notes.back: Wired Equivalent Privacy; it uses pre-shared keys with an old stream cipher and is easily broken.
notes.explanation: It was the initial Wi-Fi security protocol.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, Link-layer protection for Wi-Fi, p. 104
notes.evidence: The initial security protocol was Wired Equivalent Privacy (WEP), which was deprecated in 2004 in favor of Wi-Fi Protected Access (WPA). WEP uses 40-bit or 128-bit RC4 PSKs and is easily broken

notes.front: Where the older Wired Equivalent Privacy protocol is easily broken, WPA2 protects traffic with a mode of the {{c1::Advanced Encryption Standard}}.
notes.explanation: NIST sets the two side by side when describing Wi-Fi link-layer protection.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, Link-layer protection for Wi-Fi, p. 104
notes.evidence: WEP uses 40-bit or 128-bit RC4 PSKs and is easily broken, whereas WPA2 70 uses AES-CCM.

notes.front: An old access point’s datasheet says it supports the Wi-Fi Alliance’s interim subset of the draft 802.11i requirements, published in 2002, and nothing newer. Which certification is that?
notes.back: B: WPA.
notes.choices:
A) WPA3
B) WPA
C) Wired Equivalent Privacy
D) WPA2
notes.choicesExplained: A is the later generation that replaced the pre-shared key exchange. D is the term for equipment supporting the ratified 802.11i. C predates both and is not based on 802.11i.
notes.explanation: WPA was essentially a subset of the draft requirements available at the time.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-94, Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), 5.1.1 WLAN Standards, p. 51
notes.evidence: the Alliance created an interim solution called Wi-Fi Protected Access (WPA). Published in October 2002, WPA is essentially a subset of the draft IEEE 802.11i requirements available at that time.

notes.front: What do the Enterprise versions of WPA use for authentication instead of a pre-shared key?
notes.back: IEEE 802.1X.
notes.explanation: With 802.1X, WPA can use EAP methods such as EAP-TLS.
notes.contrast: Without 802.1X, everyone joining the network authenticates with the same pre-shared key.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, Link-layer protection for Wi-Fi, p. 104
notes.evidence: The Enterprise versions of WPA use IEEE 802.1X for authentication instead of a PSK. WPA supports a number of EAP extensions, such as EAP-TLS

notes.front: What three parties does EAP’s model use?
notes.back: A client, a server and a backend authentication, authorisation and accounting server.
notes.explanation: The server forwards messages to and from the backend server.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 3.3.2 Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP), p. 44
notes.evidence: It uses a model of a client, a server, and a backend authentication, authorization, and accounting (AAA) server. The client initiates an EAP authentication to the server. The server forwards these messages to and from the AAA server.

notes.front: Two authentication, authorisation and accounting protocols with EAP support are {{c1::RADIUS}} and Diameter.
notes.explanation: In EAP’s model, the server talks to the backend accounting and authentication server through protocols like these.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 3.3.2 Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP), p. 44
notes.evidence: AAA protocols with EAP support include Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS) [39] and Diameter [40].

notes.front: What can an attacker do once they obtain a PSK shared by a VPN server and all its remote clients?
notes.back: Impersonate any client, or the remote access VPN server itself.
notes.explanation: One secret held by everyone means one leak exposes everyone.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 3.3.4 Pre-shared Secret Key (PSK) Authentication, p. 45
notes.evidence: Once the PSK has been obtained by an attacker, it can be used to impersonate any client or the remote access VPN server itself

notes.front: A 300-person firm authenticates everyone to its office Wi-Fi with one shared passphrase, and leavers still know it. Which change moves it to per-user authentication through its RADIUS server?
notes.back: A: move to the Enterprise version, using IEEE 802.1X and EAP.
notes.choices:
A) Move to the Enterprise version, using IEEE 802.1X and EAP
B) Hide the network name
C) Change the passphrase every year
D) Switch back to Wired Equivalent Privacy
notes.choicesExplained: C still shares one secret among everyone. B does not change how users authenticate. D is deprecated and easily broken.
notes.explanation: Enterprise WPA uses 802.1X instead of a pre-shared key, so each user authenticates individually.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, Link-layer protection for Wi-Fi, p. 104
notes.evidence: The Enterprise versions of WPA use IEEE 802.1X for authentication instead of a PSK.

notes.front: What are two reasons NIST gives for WLANs typically being less secure than wired networks?
notes.back: Ease of access to the WLAN, and weak security configurations chosen to favour convenience.
notes.explanation: NIST’s WLAN guide lists these among several reasons.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-153, Guidelines for Securing Wireless Local Area Networks, Executive Summary, p. 6
notes.evidence: WLANs are typically less secure than their wired counterparts for several reasons, including the ease of access to the WLAN and the weak security configurations often used for WLANs (to favor convenience over security).

notes.front: What does NIST say a standardised security configuration for common WLAN components provides?
notes.back: A base level of security, reducing vulnerabilities and lessening the impact of successful attacks.
notes.explanation: Client devices and access points are NIST’s examples of common components.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-153, Guidelines for Securing Wireless Local Area Networks, Executive Summary, p. 6
notes.evidence: Have standardized security configurations for common WLAN components, such as client devices and APs. A standardized configuration provides a base level of security, reducing vulnerabilities and lessening the impact of successful attacks.

notes.front: A hotel group lets guests and staff share one Wi-Fi network, and guests can see staff laptops. What does NIST recommend?
notes.back: C: logically separated WLANs for external and internal use, with no connections between them.
notes.choices:
A) Turning off encryption on the guest side
B) One network with a stronger passphrase
C) Logically separated WLANs for external and internal use, with no connections between them
D) Letting guests reach any wired host they need
notes.choicesExplained: B keeps both groups on one network. A weakens security. D contradicts NIST’s advice to allow only necessary hosts and protocols.
notes.explanation: NIST says an organisation with more than one security profile for WLAN use should have separate WLANs, and devices on one should not reach devices on the other.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-153, Guidelines for Securing Wireless Local Area Networks, Executive Summary, p. 6
notes.evidence: an organization should have logically separated WLANs for external use (such as guests) and internal use. Devices on one WLAN should not be able to connect to devices on a logically separated WLAN.

notes.front: What is a “dual-connected” client device, and why is it a risk?
notes.back: A device on a wired network and a WLAN at once; wireless access to it could let an attacker reach the wired network.
notes.explanation: The wireless side becomes a path into the wired side.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-153, Guidelines for Securing Wireless Local Area Networks, Executive Summary, p. 6
notes.evidence: The term “dual connected” generally refers to a client device that is connected to both a wired network and a WLAN at the same time. If an attacker gains unauthorized wireless access to a dual-connected client device, the attacker could then use it to access or attack resources on the wired network.

notes.front: What simple action does NIST ask users to take with Bluetooth devices when they are not needed?
notes.back: Turn them off.
notes.explanation: This minimises exposure to malicious activities.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-121 Rev. 2 (Update 1), Guide to Bluetooth Security, Executive Summary, p. 7
notes.evidence: ensuring that Bluetooth devices are turned off when they are not needed to minimize exposure to malicious activities

notes.front: A commuter’s phone keeps receiving unsolicited messages over Bluetooth from a stranger nearby, urging her to add a new contact. What attack is this?
notes.back: B: bluejacking.
notes.choices:
A) Bluesnarfing
B) Bluejacking
C) A rogue base station
D) A downgrade attack
notes.choicesExplained: A forces a connection to steal stored data. D and C are cellular attacks, not Bluetooth.
notes.explanation: The messages themselves do no harm; they try to entice the user into responding or adding the contact.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-121 Rev. 2 (Update 1), Guide to Bluetooth Security, 4 Bluetooth Vulnerabilities, Threats, and Countermeasures: Bluejacking, p. 52
notes.evidence: An attacker initiates bluejacking by sending unsolicited messages to the user of a Bluetooth-enabled device. The actual messages do not cause harm to the user’s device, but they may entice the user to respond in some fashion or add the new contact

notes.front: What is one action NIST says all customers may need to take to secure their IoT products?
notes.back: Changing a default password.
notes.explanation: Product capabilities still have to be tailored to what customers can be expected to know.
notes.source: NIST IR 8259r1, Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Product Manufacturers, Background on IoT product securability, p. 10
notes.evidence: While all customers may need to take some actions to secure their IoT products (e.g., changing a default password), product cybersecurity capabilities will need to be tailored to the expected knowledge of the customer.

notes.front: IoT vulnerabilities can be eliminated by installing updates (such as patches) and by changing {{c1::configuration settings}}.
notes.explanation: Updates can also fix operational problems, improving availability, reliability and performance.
notes.source: NIST IR 8259r1, Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Product Manufacturers, Background on IoT product securability, p. 18
notes.evidence: Vulnerabilities can be eliminated by installing updates (e.g., patches) and changing configuration settings. Updates can also correct IoT product operational problems, which can improve availability, reliability, performance, and other aspects of product operation.

notes.front: A warehouse runs sensors whose default passwords cannot be changed. What compensating network control does NIST mention, and with what caveat?
notes.back: D: network segmentation, though not in all cases and not without extra cost and complexity.
notes.choices:
A) None: such devices can always be secured by policy alone
B) Disabling all logging on them
C) Connecting them to the guest WLAN
D) Network segmentation, though not in all cases and not without extra cost and complexity
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the problem NIST raises: access control is hard to enforce on such devices. C puts them among untrusted users. B removes visibility without reducing risk.
notes.explanation: NIST raises the question of how access control can be enforced on a device whose default password cannot be changed.
notes.source: NIST IR 8259r1, Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Product Manufacturers, Background on IoT product securability, p. 13
notes.evidence: how can access control be enforced if a device on the network does not allow a default password to be changed? In some instances, new controls such as network segmentation can be implemented, but not in all cases and not without additional cost and system complexity.

notes.front: A hospital receives a firmware file said to come from its infusion-pump maker. Which check does NIST give as a way to verify and authenticate such an update?
notes.back: B: code signature validation.
notes.choices:
A) Checking the file’s size
B) Code signature validation
C) Checking the file was emailed from a known address
D) Installing it on one pump to see if it works
notes.choicesExplained: A and C prove nothing about origin or integrity. D tests function, not authenticity, and risks a live device.
notes.explanation: NIST lists cryptographic hash comparison, code signature validation and manufacturer software that verifies updates automatically.
notes.source: NIST IR 8259r1, Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Product Manufacturers, Activity 8: Decide What to Communicate to Customers, p. 50
notes.evidence: Examples are cryptographic hash comparison, code signature validation, and reliance on manufacturer-provided software that automatically performs update verification and authentication.

notes.front: Why should IoT manufacturers tell customers how long updates and support will be available?
notes.back: So customers can plan to use and maintain the product securely for an appropriate length of time.
notes.explanation: The support period tells customers how long they can plan to rely on updates.
notes.source: NIST IR 8259r1, Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Product Manufacturers, Activity 8: Decide What to Communicate to Customers, p. 48
notes.evidence: Telling customers how long updates and technical support will be available may help them plan to securely use and maintain products for an appropriate amount of time.

notes.front: A council uses smart street-lighting controllers whose maker plans to declare them end of life. What does NIST suggest would help the council most?
notes.back: D: advance notice, for example six months, so it can plan.
notes.choices:
A) Silent withdrawal of updates
B) A one-day warning
C) Nothing, because end of life has no security effect
D) Advance notice, for example six months, so it can plan
notes.choicesExplained: A and B leave no time to plan retirement or a change of use. C is wrong: customers may want to retire or change how the product is used at end of life.
notes.explanation: Customers may want to retire a product, or change how it is used, when the maker considers it at end of life.
notes.source: NIST IR 8259r1, Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Product Manufacturers, Activity 8: Decide What to Communicate to Customers, p. 48
notes.evidence: Customers may want to retire a product, or at least change how the product is used, when the manufacturer considers the product and its device component at end-of-life. These customers may benefit from advance notice (e.g., six months) leading up to that endof-life so that they can plan for the event.
